title: Fast Hamiltonian engineering from cut polytope geometry
authors: Thomas Joachim Friese, Özgün Kum, Aram W. Harrow, Martin Kliesch
abstract: Hamiltonian engineering (HE) simulates quantum dynamics under a target Hamiltonian using a native entangling system Hamiltonian and restricted control, with applications from quantum gate design to analog quantum simulation. Observing that, for many systems, formulating HE as a linear program only requires specific commutation relations between the control pulses and the system Hamiltonian, we provide a unified framework for broad classes of $2$-local qubit, qudit, and fermionic systems. We reformulate time-optimal HE as a complex $k$-cut polytope problem, with $k$ the number of distinct phases in these commutation relations, and prove it NP-complete for every finite $k$. We therefore relax the polytope to the elliptope and apply a Krivine-type rounding, yielding pulses informed by the system and target Hamiltonians, which we then use in a linear program. We derive how many informed pulses are necessary and sufficient for the linear program to be reliably feasible. Additionally mixing in uniformly sampled pulses guarantees a solution close to the relaxation value from $\mathrm{O}(m)$ pulses, with $m$ the number of interaction terms. Together with upper and lower bounds on the optimal quantum run time, this yields an $\mathrm{O}(\sqrt{m})$ approximation ratio. In benchmarks on a fully connected Ising model, a chiral clock model for qudits, and the fermionic Harper-Hofstadter model, our approach attains near-optimal quantum run times wherever the optimum is computable, reaches run times that saturate with the lattice size in the fermionic case, and outperforms state-of-the-art methods with $\mathrm{O}(m)$ pulses. This establishes a unified approach with provable guarantees to the automatic programming of analog quantum simulators.
summary: This work presents a unified, mathematically rigorous framework for Hamiltonian Engineering, solving the problem of simulating a target quantum evolution using limited native controls. By reformulating the problem as an optimization over a polytope, the authors develop an efficient algorithm that achieves provable, near-optimal quantum run times. This establishes a powerful tool for the automatic design and programming of analog quantum simulators across various quantum systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses Hamiltonian Engineering (HE), which is the task of simulating a target quantum evolution ($H_{	ext{target}}$) using a native system Hamiltonian ($H_{	ext{native}}$) and controlled pulses.
main_result: The authors provide a unified framework that reformulates time-optimal HE as an NP-complete polytope problem, solving it via an elliptope relaxation and yielding an approximation ratio of $O(\sqrt{m})$ for quantum run times.
method: The core method involves reformulating the problem as a complex $k$-cut polytope optimization, relaxing it to an elliptope, and solving the resulting Linear Program (LP) using informed and mixed pulse sets.
model_or_system: The framework is applicable to broad classes of 2-local qubit, qudit, and fermionic systems, aiming to decompose the target Hamiltonian into a sum of controlled conjugations of the native Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Optimal Quantum Run Time, Approximation Ratio, Feasibility of the LP solution.
important_parameters: Number of interaction terms ($m$), number of distinct phases ($k$), and the required pulse weights ($\lambda$).
main_assumptions: The initial formulation is NP-hard, necessitating relaxation to the elliptope; the mixed LP algorithm is used to guarantee feasibility against finite pulse time errors.
figures_summary: Benchmarks are shown on a fully connected Ising model, a chiral clock model for qudits, and the fermionic Harper-Hofstadter model, demonstrating near-optimal run times.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the HE problem, proves its NP-hardness, relaxes it to an elliptope, develops the informed and mixed LP algorithms, and concludes with benchmarks comparing the approach to state-of-the-art methods.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous, provable guarantees for the automatic programming of analog quantum simulators by establishing a concrete, efficient optimization procedure for Hamiltonian decomposition.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Visualization of the solution ray and the cut polytope. All solutions lie on the intersection of the ray originating from 1, going in the direction M, and CUTn k. Better solutions lie further along the ray. The optimum is where the ray meets the boundary of CUTn k.

Figure 2: A possible projection onto the k-th roots of unity. The complex plane is cut from the origin into k equiangular sections. In counterclockwise direction, each section is assigned a k-th root of unity. Rotating the sections around the origin yields rounding functions with equivalent distributions.

Figure 3: Intuitively, one might try to solve the elliptope relaxation of the solution ray directly. Then the rounding distortion would, however, introduce a systematic devia- tion away from the ray, leading to an ineffective selection of pulses.

Figure 4: Instead of optimizing the relaxed solution ray directly, we can bend it by the inverse of the distortion function RDF◦−1 k . Then, in the rounding stage the sam- pled pulses will average out back onto the solution ray. This fully prevents the systematic deviation observed be- fore.

Figure 5: Comparison of algorithm performances on a canonical instance. The system Hamiltonian is given by an all-to-all connected Ising model on 20 qubits. The target is also an Ising-type Hamiltonian with a connec- tivity graph given by a complete bipartite graph K10,10. All couplings of both Hamiltonians are set to 1. The pulse ratio is varied over 20 equally spaced values be- tween 2.0 and 4.0. For the randomized algorithms, the data is aggregated over 50 independent runs per pulse ratio s/m.
